case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant is entitled to credit toward her supervised release term for the period during which she was actively absconding from supervision as a fugitive.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (supervised release statute), particularly subsections (a) governing imposition of supervised release terms and (i) governing extension of supervised release jurisdiction, along with related U.S. Sentencing Guidelines provisions for supervised release violations.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Isabel Rico argues that the term of supervised release legally expired by operation of law during the period she was absent, entitling her to credit for that time, and that courts lack statutory authority to toll or extend supervised release terms for absconders absent explicit congressional authorization; she further contends that the text of § 3583 does not contain a fugitive tolling exception and that any such exception must be expressly enacted by Congress rather than judicially implied, relying in part on the principle from Bowles v. Russell that courts cannot extend jurisdictional time limits beyond what statute permits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that Rico should not receive credit toward her supervised release term for the period she spent as a fugitive evading supervision, characterizing her position as an attempt to avoid consequences for drug dealing violations by exploiting her own wrongful absconding; the government contends that allowing fugitive tolling is consistent with the statute, serves the rehabilitative and protective purposes of supervised release, and prevents defendants from unilaterally terminating their supervision through flight, and further frames the question presented as whether a defendant can benefit from her own misconduct by arguing the supervised release term expired while she was deliberately evading authorities.
key_precedents: Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007) - cited by petitioner for the proposition that courts cannot extend statutory time limits beyond what Congress has authorized
United States v. Watson (Ninth Circuit) - Ninth Circuit precedent on supervised release tolling that the district court acknowledged being bound by
United States v. Pepper (Supreme Court) - cited at resentencing for the proposition that post-offense rehabilitation is relevant at resentencing hearings
Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1)(A) - referenced in Bowles v. Russell context
28 U.S.C. § 2107(a) - referenced in Bowles v. Russell context regarding appellate filing deadlines

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, but the conference deliberation has only strengthened my conviction that the structural evidence defeats it. As Justice Thomas correctly observes, if common-law background principles automatically fill statutory gaps, then Congress's express tolling in § 3624(e) and § 4210(c) would have been superfluous — the very canon Barrett invokes to support tolling actually cuts against her when applied to Congress's own drafting choices within this statute. My minimalist instincts counsel that where Congress has enacted a comprehensive supervised release scheme with specific mechanisms for post-expiration jurisdiction (§ 3583(i)) and express tolling in adjacent provisions, the institutionally appropriate course is to hold that any fugitive tolling remedy must come from Congress rather than from judicial implication of common-law doctrines with serious and unpredictable liberty consequences. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward a narrow holding focused on the structural argument — that Congress's deliberate architectural choices within the Sentencing Reform Act foreclose implied tolling — rather than a broader ruling that might unnecessarily constrain future cases involving different statutory schemes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Congress legislates against common-law background principles is the strongest counterargument, but it proves too much — if background principles automatically fill statutory gaps, then Congress's express tolling provision in § 3624(e) would have been superfluous, since the background principle would have operated there as well. The fact that Congress felt compelled to codify tolling expressly in § 3624(e) strongly suggests it did not intend to leave tolling to background common-law principles in § 3583, but rather that express authorization is required in this statutory scheme. Justice Barrett's distinction of Bowles v. Russell is creative but ultimately unpersuasive: whether we frame the question as 'extending the term' or 'declining to credit time served,' the practical effect is identical — the defendant remains subject to supervision beyond the date Congress specified, which is precisely the kind of extension Bowles prohibits without statutory authorization. The structural argument Justice Gorsuch raises — that Congress expressly addressed fugitive tolling in § 4210(c) for parole abscondment yet omitted any analogous provision from § 3583 — further confirms that this omission was deliberate, not inadvertent, and that any remedy must come from the legislature.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Congress legislates against common-law background principles remains the most serious challenge to my position, but her own reliance on § 4210(c) actually reinforces the petitioner's case: when Congress replaced parole with supervised release, it had the opportunity to carry forward express fugitive tolling and deliberately chose not to, which is precisely the kind of affirmative legislative choice that textualism requires us to respect rather than override through background-principle gap-filling. Justice Barrett's framing — that Congress didn't 'affirmatively abrogate' the common-law principle — inverts the proper inquiry in the criminal sentencing context, where the question is whether Congress affirmatively authorized courts to extend a defendant's supervision beyond the imposed term, not whether Congress prohibited them from doing so. The structural evidence Justice Thomas identifies is decisive: Congress demonstrated in § 3624(e) and § 4210(c) that it knows how to authorize tolling with precision, and its silence in § 3583 — particularly when read alongside § 3583(i)'s carefully crafted post-expiration mechanism — reflects a deliberate architectural choice that courts cannot supplement with implied equitable doctrine. The practical consequences of allowing judge-made tolling are also troubling: defendants would face indeterminate supervision periods with no clear statutory basis, creating the kind of unpredictable liberty deprivations that Congress, not courts, must authorize.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Congress legislates against common-law background principles remains the most serious challenge to my position, but after careful reflection I find it unpersuasive in this specific statutory context for reasons that align with my own judicial philosophy. The Sentencing Reform Act is a comprehensive, carefully structured statute — not a sparse common-law gap — and when Congress expressly addressed tolling in § 3624(e) and crafted the specific post-expiration jurisdictional mechanism in § 3583(i), it was not silently relying on background principles but actively making architectural choices about how supervised release disruptions would be handled. Justice Barrett's observation that Congress did not replicate § 4210(c) when it replaced parole with supervised release actually cuts against her: the more natural inference is not that Congress silently preserved common-law tolling, but that it deliberately chose a different structural approach — the § 3583(i) mechanism — rather than open-ended fugitive tolling. Most importantly, from my perspective as someone deeply attentive to the real-world impacts on vulnerable defendants, judicially implied tolling creates indeterminate supervision periods that fall hardest on those who abscond due to fear, mental illness, or domestic instability rather than calculated manipulation — and the rule of lenity demands that this ambiguity be resolved in their favor rather than through judge-made doctrine that effectively extends criminal punishment without clear congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Congress legislates against common-law background principles remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage with it directly one more time. Her point that Congress replaced parole with supervised release without replicating § 4210(c)'s express tolling — but also without affirmatively abrogating common-law fugitive tolling — has genuine force. But what ultimately persuades me to stay with the petitioner is the combination of two structural signals that Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch have sharpened: first, if background common-law principles automatically fill gaps, then § 3624(e)'s express tolling provision becomes surplusage, which the canon against surplusage disfavors; and second, Congress crafted § 3583(i) as a precise, limited post-expiration mechanism that addresses exactly the problem of late-term violations, suggesting it made a considered architectural choice about how courts may act after a term's expiration rather than leaving that space to common-law gap-filling. The liberty stakes here — indeterminate supervision periods with no textual anchor — reinforce that any tolling remedy of this kind must come from Congress, which can craft an administrable rule with clear notice to defendants.

Justice Barrett reads this as Congress leaving the common-law backdrop undisturbed, but the more natural textualist reading — consistent with the canon against surplusage — is that Congress knew exactly how to codify fugitive tolling (it had just done so in § 4210(c)) and chose not to replicate it in § 3583. The rule of lenity provides an independent and sufficient ground: where the statutory architecture leaves genuine ambiguity about whether a defendant's supervised release term can be judicially extended beyond its stated duration, that ambiguity must resolve in the defendant's favor rather than through judicial importation of common-law doctrines that effectively extend criminal punishment without congressional authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Congress legislates against common-law background principles remains the most serious challenge to my position, but after reviewing my colleagues' responses, I find the structural argument more compelling than ever. Justice Barrett's response that § 4210(c)'s parole tolling was simply not replicated in the Sentencing Reform Act actually reinforces the petitioner's position: Congress was actively restructuring the supervised release system and chose not to carry forward express tolling authority, which is precisely the kind of deliberate architectural choice that courts should respect rather than supplement through implied doctrine. My institutionalist concern remains that fashioning judge-made tolling rules in a domain where Congress has already legislated specifically — and where the liberty consequences are serious — exceeds the proper judicial role and leaves defendants subject to indeterminate supervision periods that Congress never authorized.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's surplusage argument — that if background common-law principles automatically fill gaps, then § 3624(e) and § 4210(c) would have been unnecessary — is the strongest challenge to my position, and I want to engage with it directly. But I think it misunderstands how the background-principles canon operates: Congress codifies common-law principles for clarity, emphasis, or to modify their scope, not because the principles would otherwise be inoperative. The fact that Congress expressly codified fugitive tolling for statutes of limitations in § 3290 does not render that provision surplusage — it confirms the scope and application of the principle in that specific context. More fundamentally, Justice Thomas's argument that § 4210(c)'s parole tolling provision shows Congress 'knows how to' authorize tolling actually cuts against the petitioner's position when examined carefully: that provision was enacted under the pre-SRA parole regime, and when Congress replaced parole with supervised release in 1984, the absence of an analogous provision is more naturally explained by Congress legislating against the backdrop of the common-law fugitive tolling principle than by a deliberate choice to let absconders run out the clock — particularly given that no court applying the new supervised release regime had yet confronted this precise question, making a deliberate legislative rejection of tolling implausible. I acknowledge I am alone in this position, but the strength of a legal argument is not determined by the vote count, and I believe the majority is too quick to convert Congress's silence into an affirmative prohibition.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument about common-law background principles remains the most serious challenge to my position, but I am further persuaded by the collective structural analysis my colleagues have developed: Justice Thomas's point that § 3624(e)'s express tolling provision would have been surplusage if background common-law principles automatically filled statutory gaps is particularly compelling, because it demonstrates that Congress in this very statutory scheme chose to codify tolling rather than rely on common-law incorporation. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that judicially implied tolling creates indeterminate supervision periods that defendants cannot anticipate from the sentence imposed, and the rule of lenity requires resolving this structural ambiguity in the defendant's favor rather than through judicial gap-filling that effectively extends criminal punishment without clear congressional authorization.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an express fugitive tolling provision, and Congress's deliberate choice in § 3583(i) to extend jurisdiction while letting the term run — rather than toll it — reflects a considered legislative judgment that courts should not override through implied doctrines. As the research materials note, Congress knew how to enact tolling when it wished to do so, as demonstrated by 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e), and its silence in § 3583 on fugitive tolling is therefore meaningful. Consistent with my minimalist approach and the principle from Bowles v. Russell that courts cannot extend jurisdictional time limits beyond what Congress has authorized, I would hold that judicially implied fugitive tolling in the supervised release context exceeds the proper bounds of the judicial role, particularly where Congress has already crafted a specific — if limited — mechanism in § 3583(i) for post-expiration adjudication. The narrow, textually grounded ruling here preserves institutional legitimacy by leaving any policy correction to Congress rather than permitting courts to invent parallel remedies that circumvent the limits Congress intentionally set.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 contains no express authorization for judicial tolling of supervised release terms for fugitives, and under my originalist and textualist methodology, courts cannot manufacture exceptions that Congress did not write into the statute. Congress demonstrated it knows how to authorize tolling when it wishes to do so — it expressly did so in § 3624(e) for periods of custody — yet it conspicuously omitted any fugitive tolling provision from § 3583, instead crafting the limited jurisdictional extension mechanism in § 3583(i) as its chosen remedy for late-term violations. As Bowles v. Russell makes clear, courts lack inherent authority to extend statutory time limits beyond what Congress has explicitly authorized, and the equitable appeal of preventing a defendant from benefiting from her own misconduct cannot override the constitutional separation of powers that reserves such legislative choices to Congress. The government's policy arguments, however sensible, are properly addressed to the legislature, not to this Court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an explicit fugitive tolling provision, and under my textualist approach, courts cannot manufacture equitable exceptions to statutory time limits that Congress did not authorize — a principle reinforced by Bowles v. Russell's holding that courts lack authority to extend jurisdictional deadlines beyond what statute permits. Section 3583(i) functions as a jurisdictional provision governing the court's authority over a defendant, and as the amicus brief persuasively argues, equity-based tolling doctrines cannot modify jurisdictional rules even when grounded in common-law background principles. While I am deeply sympathetic to the government's practical concern that defendants should not benefit from their own wrongdoing, Congress specifically addressed tolling during periods of custody in § 3624(e) but made no analogous provision for absconders, suggesting a deliberate legislative choice that courts should not override. The fugitive tolling doctrine as applied to supervised release absconders was not sufficiently well-settled by 1984 when § 3583 was enacted to justify reading it into the statute as an implicit background principle Congress intended to incorporate.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an explicit fugitive tolling provision, and under Bowles v. Russell, courts cannot extend statutory time limits beyond what Congress has authorized, particularly in the criminal sentencing context where liberty interests are at stake. While I am deeply sympathetic to the government's concern that defendants should not benefit from their own wrongdoing, the equitable doctrine of fugitive tolling as traditionally understood merely pauses and restarts a clock — it does not, without congressional authorization, extend a supervised release term beyond its statutory maximum or grant courts open-ended jurisdiction over defendants. The practical impact on vulnerable defendants who may abscond for reasons including fear, mental illness, or domestic instability counsels against judicially implying a tolling exception that Congress could have but did not enact, especially given that § 3583(i) already provides a specific, limited mechanism for extending jurisdiction in violation proceedings. Allowing courts to toll supervised release terms through implied equitable authority would create unpredictable, potentially indefinite supervision periods that undermine the carefully structured framework Congress designed and disproportionately harm those least able to navigate the legal system.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an explicit fugitive tolling provision, and under the principle articulated in Bowles v. Russell, courts cannot extend congressionally-imposed time limits beyond what the statute authorizes, particularly when those limits carry jurisdictional significance. While I am genuinely sympathetic to the government's equitable argument that defendants should not benefit from their own wrongdoing, the research materials themselves acknowledge that this Court has 'repeatedly held that jurisdictional statutes cannot be equitably tolled,' and if § 3583's term is jurisdictional in character, judicial implication of a tolling exception would exceed our authority regardless of its equitable appeal. Congress knows how to write tolling provisions—it has done so in other contexts—and the absence of one here is a meaningful textual signal that courts should not supply what the legislature omitted. The workable solution is to hold that any fugitive tolling remedy must come from Congress, which can craft a precise, administrable rule rather than leaving courts to develop inconsistent common-law exceptions.

The principle from Bowles v. Russell that courts cannot extend jurisdictional time limits beyond what Congress has authorized applies with force here: supervised release terms are creatures of statute, and their duration is a matter for Congress, not judicial implication, to define. While the government's common-law background principles argument has some force, the rule of lenity counsels that ambiguities in criminal statutes must be resolved in the defendant's favor, and the structural contrast between § 3583(i)'s explicit late-term violation mechanism and the absence of any abscondment tolling provision suggests Congress made a deliberate choice that courts should not override by importing judge-made exceptions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an express fugitive tolling provision, and as an institutionalist who respects the separation of powers, I am reluctant to judicially imply extensions of criminal supervision beyond what Congress has explicitly authorized. Bowles v. Russell reinforces the principle that courts should not extend statutory time limits absent clear congressional authorization, and the Sentencing Reform Act's structure—which addresses both tolling and fugitives in other provisions—suggests that Congress's silence on supervised release tolling was deliberate rather than an oversight. The proper remedy for this gap, if one exists, lies with Congress rather than with courts fashioning common-law extensions of federal criminal jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not expressly prohibit fugitive tolling, and as an originalist and textualist I must consider that Congress legislates against the backdrop of established common-law adjudicatory principles, including the longstanding principle that a fugitive should not profit from her own contumacious conduct. The absence of an express tolling provision in § 3583 does not constitute an implicit prohibition; rather, given that Congress separately addressed a different tolling dispute in § 3624(e) and resolved it in favor of more supervision, the statutory structure suggests Congress was aware of tolling principles and did not intend to displace them for absconders. Bowles v. Russell is distinguishable because it concerned a court extending a jurisdictional filing deadline beyond what Congress authorized, whereas here no court is extending the supervised release term beyond its statutory maximum but rather declining to credit time during which the defendant rendered supervision impossible through her own wrongful flight.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an explicit fugitive tolling provision, and under the rule of lenity and the principle that penal statutes must be strictly construed, courts should not imply such an exception absent clear congressional authorization. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), establishes that courts cannot extend congressionally-imposed time limits through equitable reasoning, and while the Ninth Circuit distinguished Bowles on jurisdictional grounds, that distinction is strained — if § 3583(i) sets a jurisdictional deadline, then judicially implied tolling that extends that deadline is precisely what Bowles prohibits. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that allowing courts to judicially imply tolling doctrines that extend supervision — with serious liberty consequences for defendants — without explicit statutory text creates an unprincipled regime where the scope of a defendant's sentence depends on judge-made law rather than the sentence actually imposed, undermining both procedural fairness and the notice requirements fundamental to due process. Congress knows how to enact fugitive tolling provisions, as it has done in other contexts, and its silence in § 3583 should be treated as a deliberate choice rather than an invitation for judicial gap-filling.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant is entitled to credit toward her supervised release term for the period during which she was actively absconding from supervision as a fugitive.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (supervised release statute), particularly subsections (a) governing imposition of supervised release terms and (i) governing extension of supervised release jurisdiction, as well as related sentencing guidelines provisions governing violation grades.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Isabel Rico argues that the statutory text of 18 U.S.C. § 3583 does not contain an explicit fugitive tolling provision, and therefore the supervised release term continued to run — and expired — even during the period she was absconding from supervision. She contends that courts may not judicially engraft a tolling doctrine onto the statute where Congress has not expressly provided for one, relying in part on the principle from Bowles v. Russell that courts cannot extend jurisdictional time limits beyond what Congress has authorized. Multiple amici (NACDL, National Association of Federal Defenders, Due Process Institute, MacArthur Justice Center) support this position, with the MacArthur Justice Center additionally arguing that structural barriers faced by formerly incarcerated individuals — including housing instability, lack of transportation, employment difficulties, and mental health challenges — make compliance with supervision conditions genuinely difficult and counsel against punitive tolling rules.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that Rico is not entitled to credit for time spent absconding from supervision, framing the question as whether a defendant can 'avoid any consequences from dealing drugs in violation of the terms of her supervised release by having absconded from supervision and then arguing that the term of supervised release expired while she was a fugitive.' The government contends that the Ninth Circuit precedent (Watson) correctly applies a fugitive tolling doctrine, that Rico committed a Grade A supervised release violation by possessing fentanyl (a controlled substance offense), that the California definition of fentanyl is not overbroad relative to the federal definition, and that the applicable sentencing guidelines range of 33 to 36 months (the statutory maximum) is appropriate. The government further argues that allowing supervised release terms to expire during periods of absconding would undermine the rehabilitative and supervisory purposes of the supervised release system.
key_precedents: Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007) — cited by petitioner for the proposition that courts cannot extend statutory time limits beyond what Congress has authorized
United States v. Watson (Ninth Circuit) — the circuit precedent applying fugitive tolling to supervised release terms, decided in 2011 and binding on the district court below
United States v. Pepper (Supreme Court) — cited at resentencing for the proposition that post-offense rehabilitation is relevant at resentencing hearings
Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1)(A) and 28 U.S.C. § 2107(a) — discussed in the district court's analysis of Bowles v. Russell in the appendix

Justice Thomas's expressio unius analysis and Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualist framing are both sound, but I would write an opinion that does not require every Justice to endorse the rule of lenity rationale — the structural argument alone is sufficient and more durable. A narrow opinion on these grounds preserves institutional legitimacy, signals clearly to Congress that it may legislate a more robust solution, and avoids creating doctrinal complications in adjacent areas of sentencing law.

Furthermore, § 3583(i)'s targeted post-expiration adjudication mechanism confirms that Congress addressed the fugitive problem through express textual means, leaving no room for courts to supplement with a judicially created tolling doctrine that Bowles v. The narrow, institutionally appropriate ruling here is that § 3583's silence on tolling means the supervised release term ran during the period of absconding, leaving any policy correction to the branch constitutionally empowered to make it.
